strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel technical tool: a Feynman-diagram formalism for finite-width NTK statistics, extending prior diagrammatic techniques (Banta et al. 2024, Halverson et al.) that were restricted to preactivation-only cumulants. This is a nontrivial extension since the NTK is quadratic in weights, requiring a decomposition-into-rank-four-tensors strategy rather than the Gaussian-conditional approach used previously.

The theoretical claims are backed by extensive, largely self-contained proofs (Appendices E-I) that re-derive known recursion relations from the diagrams and extend them to new results (e.g., Theorem 4.1-4.3, 5.1, 5.2), giving good confidence in correctness beyond just assertion.

Demonstrates two genuinely new results: (1) extension of finite-width preactivation stability results to the NTK/backward pass at all orders in 1/n, and (2) a proof that the diagonal NTK mean receives no finite-width corrections for scale-invariant activations (generalizing prior ReLU-specific results).

Strong empirical validation: the first-order corrected recursions are implemented for the general multi-input case (a claimed first) using an automated SymPy-to-numerical pipeline, and are shown to closely match Monte Carlo estimates from actual sampled networks for widths as small as ~20, across multiple tensors (V, A, B, D, F) and multiple activation functions (ReLU, LeakyReLU, GeLU).

Good reproducibility: detailed implementation notes, exact numerical inputs, compute resource estimates, and separate isolation of first-order correction terms (Figure 5) to directly test the theory rather than relying on the correction being swamped by the leading term.
Honest limitations section acknowledging restriction to MLPs and to low orders in 1/n, with partial verification at 1/n^2 provided as supporting evidence rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Despite the introduction motivating the work via NTK evolution during training and feature learning, the paper only computes statistics at initialization (mean/cumulants of preactivations and NTK for a fixed forward pass); no training dynamics, evolution of the NTK during optimization, or empirical connection to feature learning phenomena are demonstrated, leaving the central motivating promise of the abstract only partially delivered.

The claim that the framework 'applies to very general architectures' is asserted but not demonstrated; all derivations and experiments are restricted to simple MLPs without biases, so it remains unclear how much additional machinery (new vertices/selection rules) would be needed for attention, convolutions, or normalization layers, which limits the immediate practical relevance to modern architectures.

The extension to all orders in 1/n (Theorem 4.3) is proved somewhat schematically by appeal to 'three key facts' and pattern generalization rather than a fully worked inductive derivation with explicit new vertex definitions at arbitrary order; the 1/n^2 check in Appendix F is described as showing 'no contradictions' rather than full quantitative agreement with sampling.

Significance to the broader ICML audience may be narrow: the contribution is primarily a notational/computational simplification (replacing lengthy algebra with diagrams) for a specialist audience already versed in the effective-theory/QFT-for-NNs literature; it is unclear how this reduces to actionable insights for practitioners (e.g., no new training heuristic, generalization bound, or architecture-design recommendation is derived beyond re-deriving known stability/scale-invariance facts).

Numerical experiments use very small toy settings (4-dimensional random inputs, few distinct sample points, networks up to depth ~4-30 and modest width), so it is untested whether the diagrammatic recursions remain numerically tractable or accurate for realistic input dimensionality/dataset sizes, given the paper's own admission that naive integral evaluation is computationally expensive.

The manuscript is extremely dense with many pages of appendix-only proofs; while thorough, this places a heavy burden on readers/reviewers to verify correctness, and the main text itself provides limited intuition connecting the diagrammatic rules to concrete, checkable physical/ML meaning beyond the illustrative example in Section 4.1.

strengths: The paper extends the Feynman-diagram formalism for finite-width corrections — previously developed only for preactivation statistics (Banta et al. 2023) — to joint preactivation-NTK statistics, dNTK and ddNTK tensors, which is a genuine (if incremental) technical generalization.

A reasonably complete set of Feynman rules and selection rules is provided, and the appendix verifies by direct (tedious) derivation that the diagrammatic rules reproduce known recursion relations from Roberts & Yaida's effective theory framework, lending some credibility to the bookkeeping scheme.

The paper implements a custom SymPy-to-numerical pipeline that automatically derives and numerically solves the coupled recursion relations for the leading 1/n correction in the general multi-input case, and shows reasonable quantitative agreement with Monte Carlo-sampled finite-width networks (e.g., Figure 1), including for widths as small as ~20.

The extension of preactivation criticality/stability results to NTK-related statistics (Theorem 5.1) and the proof that scale-invariant activations leave the NTK diagonal uncorrected at finite width (Theorem 5.2) are clean, self-contained results with numerical verification.
weaknesses: Despite the introduction's heavy emphasis on finite-width effects enabling study of NTK evolution, feature learning, and training dynamics, the paper never actually analyzes training dynamics — all theory and experiments are restricted to statistics at initialization. This leaves the central motivating claim of the paper undemonstrated.

The core contribution is largely a notational/bookkeeping device for results that are, in large part, already derivable (and in several cases already derived) in Roberts & Yaida's book and related physics literature; the genuinely 'novel' items (e.g., the Θ^{1} recursion in 5.1) are not shown to yield new insight into network behavior beyond confirming known-style finite-width corrections.

The claimed 'proof' of completeness to all orders (Theorem 4.3) is a qualitative appendix sketch relying on informal statements ('this becomes evident', 'no new tensor structures arise') rather than a rigorous induction, weakening the strength of this central theoretical claim.

Experiments are confined to very shallow (4-layer) MLPs with only 4-5 fixed input points; there is no evidence the symbolic/numerical pipeline scales to realistic input-set sizes, depths, or widths, nor any discussion of the apparent combinatorial blow-up in tensor indices and Gaussian-integral dimensionality that would arise with more inputs or deeper layers.

The work is restricted entirely to bias-free MLPs; while the authors assert generalization to 'very general architectures' is conceptually straightforward, no evidence (not even a CNN or attention sketch) is given to support this claim.

The diagrammatic formalism, intended to 'dramatically simplify' computations, still requires an enormous appendix (~40 pages) of dense diagrams and selection rules to reach the same expressions obtainable (if laboriously) by direct algebra; it is unclear this actually lowers the barrier to entry for the ML community versus substituting one complex formalism for another accessible mainly to readers already fluent in QFT diagrammatics.

No comparison (quantitative or qualitative) is made to alternative finite-width NTK approaches (e.g., Hanin & Nica, Seleznova & Kutyniok, Dyer & Gur-Ari) in terms of accuracy, generality, or computational cost, making it hard to judge the practical advantage of this framework over existing alternatives.

The significance for the broader ICML audience is limited: the tool mainly offers a convenience for specialists already working within the physics-style effective-theory program, and the empirical payoff (closer agreement with finite-width Monte Carlo estimates at small widths) is a modest, somewhat expected validation of standard 1/n perturbation theory.

strengths: Rigorous, extensively documented derivation connecting Feynman diagrams to explicit algebraic recursion relations for NTK, dNTK, and ddNTK statistics, verified against prior literature (Roberts & Yaida).
Clear and well-motivated extension beyond prior diagrammatic approaches, which were restricted to preactivation statistics only.

Nontrivial theoretical results: all-order stability of NTK statistics under critical initialization, and an exact (all-order) proof that scale-invariant activations yield no finite-width correction to the NTK diagonal.

Strong empirical validation via Monte Carlo sampling of real networks, showing close agreement with theoretical predictions for NNGP, NTK, and several higher-order tensors (A, B, D, F, V) across multiple widths and criticality regimes.
First implementation of multi-input first-order finite-width NTK corrections, with a reusable symbolic-to-numerical computational pipeline.
Thorough documentation of experimental setup, proofs, and compute resources supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope limited to bias-free MLPs; extension to other architectures (CNNs, attention, residual nets) is asserted but not demonstrated.
The paper validates static initialization statistics but does not concretely demonstrate the motivating promise of capturing NTK evolution or feature learning during training.
Dense notation-heavy presentation (many colored diagram lines/rules) may limit accessibility to the broader ML audience despite the stated simplification goal.
Numerical recursion-solving is computationally expensive (up to an hour per tensor at shallow depth), with unclear scalability to deeper or larger-scale settings.
The all-orders extension (Theorem 4.3) is only lightly numerically spot-checked (D6 tensor) rather than being thoroughly validated quantitatively.
